artifact.narrative:
Mara reached the shuttered signal house before dawn, carrying the brass key her brother had died to keep from the governor. If the occupation fleet entered the narrows at sunrise, the harbor chain would trap the fishing boats alongside the warships; she meant to raise it early, even if doing so exposed her as the saboteur.

Inside, cold iron and old grease sharpened the air. Mara fitted the key into the chain-winch housing, but it stopped halfway. Fresh scratches ringed the lock. Someone had changed the wards.

“You were always going to choose the boats,” said Captain Vale from the stairwell. He held no pistol, only the missing inner gear. He wanted the fleet trapped, not destroyed: its arrival would force the council to surrender and end a siege that was starving his soldiers as surely as the town. He offered Mara the gear if she would wait until the last fishing boat cleared the narrows.

She heard boots gathering below. Waiting meant capture; refusing meant Vale could drop the gear through the floor grate and make the chain useless. Mara pulled the bell rope instead. Its first stroke boomed across the black water—the forbidden storm signal her brother had taught every harbor child to obey. Vale seized her wrist, but she wound the rope around the winch and threw her weight backward. The second stroke sounded raggedly as soldiers burst through the door.

Lanterns flared aboard the fishing boats. One by one, they turned for the marsh channels rather than the narrows. Vale understood too late: Mara had never needed to raise the chain first. She needed the civilians to move.

He released her and slammed the gear onto the workbench. “Now we both hang.”

“Only if they take the house.” Mara seated the gear while Vale barred the door. Below them, axes struck wood. Above, the final bell stroke rolled toward the fleet, and the winch teeth caught with a heavy, promising click.
artifact.title: The Bell-Rope Test
